full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I agree with the first pass. What you saw is the low-b, cooperator-dominated, nearly frozen state of the Nowak–May spatial Prisoner's Dilemma. Defectors survive only as small pockets or line fragments, and the cells along those fragments keep flipping. Rule 2 only pushes the lattice further toward cooperators; it adds no new behaviour.

**The base model is Nowak–May, unchanged.** Rule 1 is their 1992 setup: each cell plays the PD game with nearest neighboring sites and with one's own site (thus we define these sites as a territory – a 3x3 grid), then copies the best scorer. Your payoffs (R=1, P=S=0, T=1.3) are their simplified, rescaled payoff matrix ... which only contains one free parameter b, with b = 1.3.

**b = 1.3 is not the chaotic window.** They found that for b < 1.8 big D cluster will shrink, while for b < 2, 2x2 or larger cluster of C will continue to grow. A review reproducing the model shows stationary 80 × 80 patterns started from random states at several b values. It marks sites invaded in the last step, which is how the flipping cells show up. It also describes the mechanism behind them: defectors that invade then score poorly against each other, and they flip back to cooperation. Wu, Fu and Wang describe the same picture at higher b: cooperators quickly cluster and thus press defectors into line fragments. Strategy switching just happens along these line fragments.

**How each measured feature fits:**
- **g_largest_domain ≈ 0.94** and **g_moran ≈ 0.57**: cooperators fill most of the lattice and form a strong cluster, as expected at low b.
- **g_reversals = 1**: this is the flipping along the edges of the defector fragments (blinkers), which is documented.
- **Low g_n_domains, g_corrlen = 3**: a few small leftover defector pockets.
- **Rule 1 alone** already reproduces every feature (largest domain 0.89, Moran 0.56, reversals 1, corrlen 2). Adding rule 2 just moves the numbers slightly further toward cooperators.

**Rule 2 is a twist in the rules, not in the behaviour.** It only ever turns defectors into cooperators. Run alone, it drives the lattice to all-cooperator with no structure (largest domain 1.0, Moran 0). The closest documented extension, Mukherji et al. (1996), adds noise in the opposite direction: each cooperator has a small independent probability, ϕ, of cheating by switching to defection. A one-way push toward cooperators can only help a takeover the game already favours. I found no new phenomenology from it.

**Genuine or artifact?** The clustering is a real effect of the game, so this isn't a random colouring or a numerical failure. But it's close to frozen: a mostly settled pattern with a few blinking sites. Two things make the knock-out comparison look more impressive than it is. The knock-out of rule 1 leaves an uncorrelated random lattice, so almost any clustering beats it. And with rule 2 kept, that baseline would slowly drift toward all-cooperator. The cooperator-majority labelling is also partly odd: rule-2-only scores largest domain 1.0 while scoring 0 for domain count, correlation length and Moran.
